extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental physicists and mathematicians studying mechanics, projectile motion, and fluid resistance (readers of Philosophical Transactions)
extracted.subtask_description: Mathematical modelling and experimental guidance for studying the resistance of fluids on moving bodies (projectiles, falling bodies, pendula), including how to represent successive abatements of force, how to construct the resulting trajectories, and what experiments are needed to determine resistance laws and parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance is not purely proportional to square of velocity (must be determined experimentally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although in an ideal fluid the resistance would be proportional to the square of the velocity, real fluids add other resistance forces (due to tenacity/viscosity, compression of the medium, friction), so the total resistance is 'probably to be expounded by some compound function of the velocity, the discovery of which must chiefly depend on proper experiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume only the duplicate ratio law; design experiments to discover the actual functional dependence of resistance on velocity, including additional components from medium compression, tenacity and friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for weight/compression and tenacity/friction of the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: A body moving through the atmosphere must not only remove particles (giving a square-of-velocity resistance) but also overcome the weight by which particles are compressed together, and possibly tenacity and friction; these add another force of resistance that does not follow the same law as the square term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models and experiments should include terms or factors representing the medium's compression (effective weight), internal cohesion (tenacity), and frictional effects; compare behaviour across media with differing viscous/tenacious properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model successive abatement of impressed force as a decreasing geometric progression
rubrics_metrics.description: The remaining (effective) force after each equal moment is proportionally reduced, producing a continuously decreasing geometric progression for successive moments; the aggregate of these terms is finite and calculable (sum of geometric series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modelling motion in a resisting medium, represent the sequence of effective impulses/velocities over equal time intervals as a geometric series and use series-sum formulae to compute finite displacements and limiting behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent the infinite decreasing progression geometrically via an exterior hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: The infinite decreasing geometric progression of successive dispatched lengths can be fitly expressed by an ordinate in the exterior hyperbola parallel to an asymptote; the members of the progression correspond to segments cut in continual proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the hyperbolic geometric construction (ordinates and asymptotes) as a visual/mathematical representation linking the series terms to curve geometry when deriving trajectories under resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: For descent, replace arithmetic increments by decreasing geometric progression under resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: In free fall without resistance, successive impulses produce arithmetical progression (1, 1+1, 1+1+1…). With air resistance, each of these equal progressions must be substituted by a decreasing geometric progression analogous to the projection case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing descent in a resisting medium, model the continual increments (which would be arithmetic without resistance) as geometric terms determined by the resistance parameter; derive the series terms accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine impressed force and gravity algebraically to get net ascent/descent rates
rubrics_metrics.description: For a body projected vertically, the rate of ascent or descent is obtained by adding (projection downward) or subtracting (projection upward) the geometric-series terms representing the impressed force and the impulse of gravity; when the decreasing (impressed) and increasing (gravity impulses) parts equal, ascent ceases and descent begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose the series for impressed force and for gravity appropriately (addition or subtraction) to determine instantaneous and long-term motion; solve for the point where net series sum changes sign to find maxima of ascent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and construct the 'linea projectorum' (trajectory) for projectiles in resisting media
rubrics_metrics.description: The curve produced by the compound of motion in the line of projection and descent, with their respective (decreasing) geometric increments, is the 'linea projectorum', a parabola-deformed curve; the celerity and tendency at each point are determined by the tangent, and the greatest percussion occurs normal to that tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine the instantaneous motion and impact directions for projectiles in resistant media, construct the trajectory by fitting ordinates whose increments follow the specified geometric proportions and use tangents/normals to read velocities and points of maximum strike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the resistance parameter (proportion m:1) by experiment and scale to other forces/media
rubrics_metrics.description: The precise proportion of m to 1 (or the resistance parameter that defines the geometric ratio) 'remains to be inquired by experiment.' Once found for one known force and medium, the same proportion can be used for other forces or mediums if their relative proportions are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to measure the resistance parameter for a given body and medium; use measured ratios to extrapolate to other forces and, when possible, to other media provided relative resistances/densities are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for body shape, orientation and specific gravity when predicting resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Different bodies encounter different resistance in the same medium according to their gravities, figures, and positions in motion (e.g., a sharp arrow penetrates more easily than a blunt bolt; orientation such as point-first vs base-forward changes resistance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental designs and theoretical models must include geometric shape and orientation factors and consider specific gravity (density) of the moving body as modulators of resistance; avoid treating bodies of differing form or orientation as equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: If media are equally fluid and other circumstances alike, resistance scales with intensive gravity of the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Different mediums equally fluid, other circumstances being alike, resist in proportion to their intensive gravity, because a heavier medium presents more mass to be removed by the same force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing media of similar fluidity, use intensive gravity (density) as a scaling factor for resistance in models and experiments; nevertheless, check for confounding viscous/tenacious differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pendulum experiments to quantify air's opposition and verify theoretical speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposition of the medium and its effects on pendulum vibrations are considered, and several pendulum experiments are described 'in order to verify the foregoing speculation, and to determine the quantity of the air's opposition to bodies moving in it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct controlled pendulum experiments (varying amplitude, mass, shape, and medium) to estimate air resistance; use empirical measurements to calibrate theoretical terms for damping and opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine density distribution of the medium to produce assigned trajectories (inverse problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general method is laid down for determining the density of the medium in all places which, together with uniform gravity, will make a projectile move in any assigned curve; this is applied to circular motion and conditions under which circles become proportional spirals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the medium-density distribution as a design parameter: use inverse methods to compute what spatial density profile would be required to yield a desired trajectory, and test such constructions where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge experimental and computational limitations and allow for approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes some objections to points of the process and suppositions, stating that avoiding them would make computations much more perplexed; in matters so nice and dependent on physical observations it will be hard to attain such accuracy as not to stand in need of some allowances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting experiments or complex computations, plan for approximation, error margins, and pragmatic simplifications; design follow-up experiments after deliberation to refine parameters rather than overcomplicating initial analyses.
